Professional line-standing becomes growing business as Americans seek to skip waits
January 16, 2026
(InvestigateTV) — If you don’t want to stand in line, you might be able to hire someone to do it for you.
A recent study found 85% of U.S. consumers wait in line at least a few times a month, and 65% describe negative emotions such as boredom, impatience and frustration from the experience.
Companies are now capitalizing on that frustration by offering professional line-standing services.
Rick Piel is a professional linestander in Washington, D.C.
When we tagged along with him on a recent gig, he arrived at the Washington Monument at 6:20 a.m. on a Tuesday morning.
He aims to be among the first people at the popular destination to secure free tickets that are released daily at 9 a.m. on a first-come, first-served basis.
“The line will get very long. There’ll be hundreds of people here and they only give out 200 tickets,” Piel said.
Piel works for Skip the Line, a Washington, D.C.-based company founded by Jennifer Goff in 2017. Goff started the business after noticing a massive line outside a “Game of Thrones” pop-up bar.
“It was more of an experiment to see if people would actually hire me,” Goff said. “But as soon as it happened, I just felt like this jolt of energy where I could really take this to the next level if I really worked really hard to do so.”
The company now employs a team of linestanders who wait for restaurant reservations, book signings, limited release product launches and general admission tickets to concerts and museums.
In Washington, D.C., frequent requests involve waiting for congressional hearings and Supreme Court cases with limited public seating.
Customers pay between $30 and $40 per hour for the service, with higher rates for overnight waits and during harsh weather conditions.
The home services platform TaskRabbit also offers waiting in line as a paid task. From 2023 to 2024, the company reported an 18% increase in bookings for that service nationwide.
Dr. Maggie Mulqueen, a Massachusetts-based psychologist, wrote an opinion piece for CNN in 2023 arguing there’s value in delayed gratification and questioning when waiting got such a negative reputation.
“I’m not saying everything is worth waiting for, but there are certain things in life that I think actually increase in value,” Mulqueen said. “I mean, if Christmas was every day, it wouldn’t be Christmas.”
Mulqueen expressed concerns about fairness and perceived inequities in society.
“We have commodified waiting so much that the people who don’t have to wait look down on the people who are waiting,” she said. “The haves and the have nots.”
Goff said her company emphasizes transparency about its services. For concerts, linestanders can hold spots for up to three people, and they inform those behind them in line.
“We always make sure clients know, hey, once you swap with us, please don’t bring 10 other people up front in line with you because it also hurts our business and our branding,” Goff said.
At the Washington Monument, other people waiting in line expressed no complaints about Piel’s paid service.
“It’s fine with me,” said Jerry Bennington, who was waiting in line. “I mean, you gotta make money somehow.”
Piel said his longest linestanding assignment lasted 138 hours for a high-profile Supreme Court case.
Skip the Line has also received requests for Fourth of July parade seating and even holding parking spots for clients.

A Portland Teenager Found a $3 Lakers Jacket at Goodwill. He’s About to Make a Quarter of a Million Dollars.
June 27, 2026 8:38AM PDT
It’s the kind of Goodwill score thrifters dream about.
Back in January, Portland teenager Quinn Brown found a Wilt Chamberlain Los Angeles Lakers warm-up jacket in the Goodwill Bins. It cost $3.07. Brown suspected it was the real deal, though, based on its worn appearance and some online photo-sleuthing. The stitch patterns seemed to match the jacket the NBA star wore during the 1972 Finals.
He was right.
The gold-and-purple short-sleeved jacket was professionally authenticated and it’s going up for auction at Sotheby’s New York starting July 1. It’s estimated it will fetch $150,000 to $250,000, according to the auction house, which calls the jacket “rare and significant.”
“This jacket is an extraordinary piece of memorabilia from Chamberlain’s final chapter in the NBA,” Sotheby’s writes in its promotional materials for the “Summer Sports Marquee” auction.
A similar Chamberlain warm-up jacket, worn during the 1968–69 season, sold in 2022 for $56,400 at Heritage Auctions. A representative from that auction house says the market has sweetened since then, as Wilt Chamberlain gear has proven to be some of the most coveted NBA memorabilia. In 2023, Chamberlain’s 1972 Finals jersey sold for $4.9 million at Sotheby’s. That’s the third-most expensive NBA jersey ever sold at auction, behind only Kobe Bryant and Michael Jordan jerseys. Though he played a few years before those superstars, Chamberlain is known as one of the 10 greatest basketball players of all time, and still holds the single-game scoring record of 100 points, set in 1962.
Brown, a 19-year-old Lincoln High School graduate, found the jacket at one of the three metro-area Goodwill Outlet locations. He would not reveal which. “I don’t want a ton of people to start coming there,” he says.
It’s a mystery how the jacket made its way to the Portland-area Goodwill Outlets. Goodwill Industries of the Columbia Willamette operates Goodwill Outlets, as they are officially known, in Northeast Portland, Hillsboro, Milwaukie and Vancouver, Wash. They’re called the “Bins” after the large, rolling blue bins that shoppers can pick through; most clothes are sold by the pound.
Each location has communities of “pickers” like Brown who have an eye for valuable merchandise and know how to work the resale market. Shopping at the bins is like a grody, competitive treasure hunt—an experience that separates the real-deal pickers from the ones who are more into curated vintage boutiques.
Brown learned the trade from his older sister and has been reselling his finds for about three years, mostly on Depop and a little on eBay.
It was a normal weekday morning Jan. 15 at the Bins until the staff did one of their regular merchandise rotations at 10 am.
“They brought in the new clothes, and for about five minutes I’m looking through with around 20 to 30 people, trying to pick some stuff out,” Brown says. “I see this guy with a cool Lakers jacket. He looked a year or two older than I am; maybe he resells, maybe he doesn’t. Suddenly, he tosses it back and I immediately grabbed it because I could tell it was good.”
The warmup jacket is short-sleeved, collared and Lakers yellow, with a team logo on the chest and “Chamberlain” stitched across the back in purple.
From there, the research began. There are no tags, size or anything like that, which makes sense given the time period and that it was custom made. Brown started comparing photos of the jersey with photos of Chamberlain at games online, analyzing stitching and patches. The jacket’s Scovill buttons, which were popular on uniforms until they were discontinued in 1984, were another sign of authenticity.
Pretty quickly, Brown learned from others in the resale industry that the next step was to get the jacket authenticated. Within a week, multiple auction houses were interested. Brown chose Sotheby’s, which handled the authentication process.
The authenticator, SIA Photo Match, matched the jacket in February to photos taken of Chamberlain during three Lakers games, including one game during the 1972 NBA Finals, a series in which the Lakers defeated the New York Knicks. Brown woke up to a message from Sotheby’s about the 1972 Finals photo match and immediately knew the value had just skyrocketed.
“That was the most exciting moment I’ve had in my life.”
Before finding the Chamberlain jersey, Brown’s biggest Goodwill score was a vintage Sub Pop T-shirt that said “LOSER” on the front. It sold for $250 on Depop. Since graduating from Lincoln, he has stayed in town to focus on his thrifting business. “I’ve just been getting better and better at it.”
Brown intends to invest his earnings from the auction in either an index fund or real estate. First, he’ll use some of the money on a trip to Vietnam with friends a few weeks after the auction closes July 20.
“This is a crazy experience,” Brown said shortly after the big find. “A couple of days ago I had found nothing crazy, then this. It’s amazing.”

Eggonomics: Rising egg prices means big business for chicken rentals
March 4, 2025
As egg prices continue to rise, more people are considering backyard chickens as a way to secure their own egg supply.
For Wendy Hyland, renting hens has been a summer tradition for the past three years, although she is an empty nester through the winter.
“You get to experience having chickens, taking care of them,” Hyland said. “But when it’s cold, they come, and they pick them up.”
Hyland rents her hens through Rent the Chicken, a company that provides temporary backyard flocks, including shelter, food, supplies, and even treats. The program also allows participants to "chicken out" if they decide backyard farming isn't for them.
With egg prices rising, Hyland is considering doubling her flock this year. Renting two hens for six months costs $545, while four hens cost $795. The four-hen package provides about 48 dozen eggs over the rental period — roughly the same amount that would cost $480 at current grocery store prices.
Jenn Tompkins, co-owner of Rent the Chicken, said demand has increased as shoppers look for alternatives to expensive and scarce store-bought eggs.
“They don’t have to worry about the prices of eggs in-store,” Tompkins said. “They don’t have to worry about if there are eggs at the store or if they have to limit egg purchasing because they have their food source in their own backyard.”
Tompkins added that with such a small flock of two or four, bird flu is a lot less of a concern. But her company provides education and support if anyone has questions.
Mike Slavin, who sells and rents chicken coops at Slavins Buildings in Ohio, said he's seen a surge in interest as well.
“Ever since these egg prices have taken off, going to $5 a dozen, I’ve been getting many phone calls on chicken coops,” Slavin said.
He offers a rent-to-own option, with a 6-by-8-foot coop costing $2,800 to buy or $118 per month to rent. About 40% of his customers choose rent-to-own to avoid paying upfront costs.
"Right now, chicken coops are a little harder to get," Slavin said. "But we've seen more being built right now because of the egg prices."
Hyland admits she likely doesn't save money with her birds, especially with a household full of egg eaters.
“Probably will be a wash… because I have a lot of egg eaters that go through them very quickly,” she said.
Still, she enjoys the experience — so much so that she spoils her hens with extra treats and even toys.
For those considering backyard chickens, now may be the time to act. Demand for rentals and coops is high, and suppliers expect to sell out as spring approaches.
This story was originally published by Elizabeth VanMetre with the Scripps News Group.

Brown suspected it was the real deal, though, based on its worn appearance and some online photo-sleuthing. The stitch patterns seemed to match the jacket the NBA star wore during the 1972 Finals.
He was right.
The gold-and-purple short-sleeved jacket was professionally authenticated and it’s going up for auction at Sotheby’s New York starting July 1. It’s estimated it will fetch $150,000 to $250,000, according to the auction house, which calls the jacket “rare and significant.”
“This jacket is an extraordinary piece of memorabilia from Chamberlain’s final chapter in the NBA,” Sotheby’s writes in its promotional materials for the “Summer Sports Marquee” auction.
A similar Chamberlain warm-up jacket, worn during the 1968–69 season, sold in 2022 for $56,400 at Heritage Auctions. A representative from that auction house says the market has sweetened since then, as Wilt Chamberlain gear has proven to be some of the most coveted NBA memorabilia. In 2023, Chamberlain’s 1972 Finals jersey sold for $4.9 million at Sotheby’s. That’s the third-most expensive NBA jersey ever sold at auction, behind only Kobe Bryant and Michael Jordan jerseys. Though he played a few years before those superstars, Chamberlain is known as one of the 10 greatest basketball players of all time, and still holds the single-game scoring record of 100 points, set in 1962.
Brown, a 19-year-old Lincoln High School graduate, found the jacket at one of the three metro-area Goodwill Outlet locations. He would not reveal which. “I don’t want a ton of people to start coming there,” he says.
It’s a mystery how the jacket made its way to the Portland-area Goodwill Outlets. Goodwill Industries of the Columbia Willamette operates Goodwill Outlets, as they are officially known, in Northeast Portland, Hillsboro, Milwaukie and Vancouver, Wash. They’re called the “Bins” after the large, rolling blue bins that shoppers can pick through; most clothes are sold by the pound.
Each location has communities of “pickers” like Brown who have an eye for valuable merchandise and know how to work the resale market. Shopping at the bins is like a grody, competitive treasure hunt—an experience that separates the real-deal pickers from the ones who are more into curated vintage boutiques.
Brown learned the trade from his older sister and has been reselling his finds for about three years, mostly on Depop and a little on eBay.
It was a normal weekday morning Jan. 15 at the Bins until the staff did one of their regular merchandise rotations at 10 am.
“They brought in the new clothes, and for about five minutes I’m looking through with around 20 to 30 people, trying to pick some stuff out,” Brown says. “I see this guy with a cool Lakers jacket. He looked a year or two older than I am; maybe he resells, maybe he doesn’t. Suddenly, he tosses it back and I immediately grabbed it because I could tell it was good.”
The warmup jacket is short-sleeved, collared and Lakers yellow, with a team logo on the chest and “Chamberlain” stitched across the back in purple.
From there, the research began. There are no tags, size or anything like that, which makes sense given the time period and that it was custom made. Brown started comparing photos of the jersey with photos of Chamberlain at games online, analyzing stitching and patches. The jacket’s Scovill buttons, which were popular on uniforms until they were discontinued in 1984, were another sign of authenticity.
Pretty quickly, Brown learned from others in the resale industry that the next step was to get the jacket authenticated. Within a week, multiple auction houses were interested. Brown chose Sotheby’s, which handled the authentication process.
The authenticator, SIA Photo Match, matched the jacket in February to photos taken of Chamberlain during three Lakers games, including one game during the 1972 NBA Finals, a series in which the Lakers defeated the New York Knicks. Brown woke up to a message from Sotheby’s about the 1972 Finals photo match and immediately knew the value had just skyrocketed.
“That was the most exciting moment I’ve had in my life.”

Eggonomics: Rising egg prices means big business for chicken rentals
March 4, 2025
As egg prices continue to rise, more people are considering backyard chickens as a way to secure their own egg supply.
For Wendy Hyland, renting hens has been a summer tradition for the past three years, although she is an empty nester through the winter.
“You get to experience having chickens, taking care of them,” Hyland said. “But when it’s cold, they come, and they pick them up.”
Hyland rents her hens through Rent the Chicken, a company that provides temporary backyard flocks, including shelter, food, supplies, and even treats. The program also allows participants to "chicken out" if they decide backyard farming isn't for them.
With egg prices rising, Hyland is considering doubling her flock this year. Renting two hens for six months costs $545, while four hens cost $795. The four-hen package provides about 48 dozen eggs over the rental period — roughly the same amount that would cost $480 at current grocery store prices.
Jenn Tompkins, co-owner of Rent the Chicken, said demand has increased as shoppers look for alternatives to expensive and scarce store-bought eggs.
“They don’t have to worry about the prices of eggs in-store,” Tompkins said. “They don’t have to worry about if there are eggs at the store or if they have to limit egg purchasing because they have their food source in their own backyard.”
Tompkins added that with such a small flock of two or four, bird flu is a lot less of a concern. But her company provides education and support if anyone has questions.
Mike Slavin, who sells and rents chicken coops at Slavins Buildings in Ohio, said he's seen a surge in interest as well.
“Ever since these egg prices have taken off, going to $5 a dozen, I’ve been getting many phone calls on chicken coops,” Slavin said.
He offers a rent-to-own option, with a 6-by-8-foot coop costing $2,800 to buy or $118 per month to rent. About 40% of his customers choose rent-to-own to avoid paying upfront costs.
"Right now, chicken coops are a little harder to get," Slavin said. "But we've seen more being built right now because of the egg prices."
Hyland admits she likely doesn't save money with her birds, especially with a household full of egg eaters.
“Probably will be a wash… because I have a lot of egg eaters that go through them very quickly,” she said.
Still, she enjoys the experience — so much so that she spoils her hens with extra treats and even toys.
For those considering backyard chickens, now may be the time to act. Demand for rentals and coops is high, and suppliers expect to sell out as spring approaches.
This story was originally published by Elizabeth VanMetre with the Scripps News Group.

A Portland Teenager Found a $3 Lakers Jacket at Goodwill. He’s About to Make a Quarter of a Million Dollars.
June 27, 2026 8:38AM PDT
It’s the kind of Goodwill score thrifters dream about.
Back in January, Portland teenager Quinn Brown found a Wilt Chamberlain Los Angeles Lakers warm-up jacket in the Goodwill Bins. It cost $3.07. Brown suspected it was the real deal, though, based on its worn appearance and some online photo-sleuthing. The stitch patterns seemed to match the jacket the NBA star wore during the 1972 Finals.
He was right.
The gold-and-purple short-sleeved jacket was professionally authenticated and it’s going up for auction at Sotheby’s New York starting July 1. It’s estimated it will fetch $150,000 to $250,000, according to the auction house, which calls the jacket “rare and significant.”
“This jacket is an extraordinary piece of memorabilia from Chamberlain’s final chapter in the NBA,” Sotheby’s writes in its promotional materials for the “Summer Sports Marquee” auction.
A similar Chamberlain warm-up jacket, worn during the 1968–69 season, sold in 2022 for $56,400 at Heritage Auctions. A representative from that auction house says the market has sweetened since then, as Wilt Chamberlain gear has proven to be some of the most coveted NBA memorabilia. In 2023, Chamberlain’s 1972 Finals jersey sold for $4.9 million at Sotheby’s. That’s the third-most expensive NBA jersey ever sold at auction, behind only Kobe Bryant and Michael Jordan jerseys. Though he played a few years before those superstars, Chamberlain is known as one of the 10 greatest basketball players of all time, and still holds the single-game scoring record of 100 points, set in 1962.
Brown, a 19-year-old Lincoln High School graduate, found the jacket at one of the three metro-area Goodwill Outlet locations. He would not reveal which. “I don’t want a ton of people to start coming there,” he says.
It’s a mystery how the jacket made its way to the Portland-area Goodwill Outlets. Goodwill Industries of the Columbia Willamette operates Goodwill Outlets, as they are officially known, in Northeast Portland, Hillsboro, Milwaukie and Vancouver, Wash. They’re called the “Bins” after the large, rolling blue bins that shoppers can pick through; most clothes are sold by the pound.
Each location has communities of “pickers” like Brown who have an eye for valuable merchandise and know how to work the resale market. Shopping at the bins is like a grody, competitive treasure hunt—an experience that separates the real-deal pickers from the ones who are more into curated vintage boutiques.
Brown learned the trade from his older sister and has been reselling his finds for about three years, mostly on Depop and a little on eBay.
It was a normal weekday morning Jan. 15 at the Bins until the staff did one of their regular merchandise rotations at 10 am.
“They brought in the new clothes, and for about five minutes I’m looking through with around 20 to 30 people, trying to pick some stuff out,” Brown says. “I see this guy with a cool Lakers jacket. He looked a year or two older than I am; maybe he resells, maybe he doesn’t. Suddenly, he tosses it back and I immediately grabbed it because I could tell it was good.”
The warmup jacket is short-sleeved, collared and Lakers yellow, with a team logo on the chest and “Chamberlain” stitched across the back in purple.
From there, the research began. There are no tags, size or anything like that, which makes sense given the time period and that it was custom made. Brown started comparing photos of the jersey with photos of Chamberlain at games online, analyzing stitching and patches. The jacket’s Scovill buttons, which were popular on uniforms until they were discontinued in 1984, were another sign of authenticity.
Pretty quickly, Brown learned from others in the resale industry that the next step was to get the jacket authenticated. Within a week, multiple auction houses were interested. Brown chose Sotheby’s, which handled the authentication process.
The authenticator, SIA Photo Match, matched the jacket in February to photos taken of Chamberlain during three Lakers games, including one game during the 1972 NBA Finals, a series in which the Lakers defeated the New York Knicks. Brown woke up to a message from Sotheby’s about the 1972 Finals photo match and immediately knew the value had just skyrocketed.
“That was the most exciting moment I’ve had in my life.”
Before finding the Chamberlain jersey, Brown’s biggest Goodwill score was a vintage Sub Pop T-shirt that said “LOSER” on the front. It sold for $250 on Depop. Since graduating from Lincoln, he has stayed in town to focus on his thrifting business. “I’ve just been getting better and better at it.”
Brown intends to invest his earnings from the auction in either an index fund or real estate. First, he’ll use some of the money on a trip to Vietnam with friends a few weeks after the auction closes July 20.
“This is a crazy experience,” Brown said shortly after the big find. “A couple of days ago I had found nothing crazy, then this. It’s amazing.”

Professional line-standing becomes growing business as Americans seek to skip waits
January 16, 2026
(InvestigateTV) — If you don’t want to stand in line, you might be able to hire someone to do it for you.
A recent study found 85% of U.S. consumers wait in line at least a few times a month, and 65% describe negative emotions such as boredom, impatience and frustration from the experience.
Companies are now capitalizing on that frustration by offering professional line-standing services.
Rick Piel is a professional linestander in Washington, D.C.
When we tagged along with him on a recent gig, he arrived at the Washington Monument at 6:20 a.m. on a Tuesday morning.
He aims to be among the first people at the popular destination to secure free tickets that are released daily at 9 a.m. on a first-come, first-served basis.
“The line will get very long. There’ll be hundreds of people here and they only give out 200 tickets,” Piel said.
Piel works for Skip the Line, a Washington, D.C.-based company founded by Jennifer Goff in 2017. Goff started the business after noticing a massive line outside a “Game of Thrones” pop-up bar.
“It was more of an experiment to see if people would actually hire me,” Goff said. “But as soon as it happened, I just felt like this jolt of energy where I could really take this to the next level if I really worked really hard to do so.”
The company now employs a team of linestanders who wait for restaurant reservations, book signings, limited release product launches and general admission tickets to concerts and museums.
In Washington, D.C., frequent requests involve waiting for congressional hearings and Supreme Court cases with limited public seating.
Customers pay between $30 and $40 per hour for the service, with higher rates for overnight waits and during harsh weather conditions.
The home services platform TaskRabbit also offers waiting in line as a paid task. From 2023 to 2024, the company reported an 18% increase in bookings for that service nationwide.
Dr. Maggie Mulqueen, a Massachusetts-based psychologist, wrote an opinion piece for CNN in 2023 arguing there’s value in delayed gratification and questioning when waiting got such a negative reputation.
“I’m not saying everything is worth waiting for, but there are certain things in life that I think actually increase in value,” Mulqueen said. “I mean, if Christmas was every day, it wouldn’t be Christmas.”
Mulqueen expressed concerns about fairness and perceived inequities in society.
“We have commodified waiting so much that the people who don’t have to wait look down on the people who are waiting,” she said. “The haves and the have nots.”
Goff said her company emphasizes transparency about its services. For concerts, linestanders can hold spots for up to three people, and they inform those behind them in line.
“We always make sure clients know, hey, once you swap with us, please don’t bring 10 other people up front in line with you because it also hurts our business and our branding,” Goff said.
At the Washington Monument, other people waiting in line expressed no complaints about Piel’s paid service.
“It’s fine with me,” said Jerry Bennington, who was waiting in line. “I mean, you gotta make money somehow.”
Piel said his longest linestanding assignment lasted 138 hours for a high-profile Supreme Court case.
Skip the Line has also received requests for Fourth of July parade seating and even holding parking spots for clients.

Eggonomics: Rising egg prices means big business for chicken rentals
March 4, 2025
As egg prices continue to rise, more people are considering backyard chickens as a way to secure their own egg supply.
For Wendy Hyland, renting hens has been a summer tradition for the past three years, although she is an empty nester through the winter.
“You get to experience having chickens, taking care of them,” Hyland said. “But when it’s cold, they come, and they pick them up.”
Hyland rents her hens through Rent the Chicken, a company that provides temporary backyard flocks, including shelter, food, supplies, and even treats. The program also allows participants to "chicken out" if they decide backyard farming isn't for them.
With egg prices rising, Hyland is considering doubling her flock this year. Renting two hens for six months costs $545, while four hens cost $795. The four-hen package provides about 48 dozen eggs over the rental period — roughly the same amount that would cost $480 at current grocery store prices.
Jenn Tompkins, co-owner of Rent the Chicken, said demand has increased as shoppers look for alternatives to expensive and scarce store-bought eggs.
“They don’t have to worry about the prices of eggs in-store,” Tompkins said. “They don’t have to worry about if there are eggs at the store or if they have to limit egg purchasing because they have their food source in their own backyard.”
Tompkins added that with such a small flock of two or four, bird flu is a lot less of a concern. But her company provides education and support if anyone has questions.
Mike Slavin, who sells and rents chicken coops at Slavins Buildings in Ohio, said he's seen a surge in interest as well.
“Ever since these egg prices have taken off, going to $5 a dozen, I’ve been getting many phone calls on chicken coops,” Slavin said.
He offers a rent-to-own option, with a 6-by-8-foot coop costing $2,800 to buy or $118 per month to rent. About 40% of his customers choose rent-to-own to avoid paying upfront costs.
"Right now, chicken coops are a little harder to get," Slavin said. "But we've seen more being built right now because of the egg prices."
Hyland admits she likely doesn't save money with her birds, especially with a household full of egg eaters.
“Probably will be a wash… because I have a lot of egg eaters that go through them very quickly,” she said.
Still, she enjoys the experience — so much so that she spoils her hens with extra treats and even toys.
For those considering backyard chickens, now may be the time to act. Demand for rentals and coops is high, and suppliers expect to sell out as spring approaches.
This story was originally published by Elizabeth VanMetre with the Scripps News Group.

Рик Пиль из фирмы Skip the Line за деньги стоит в очередях. Вход в монумент Вашингтона бесплатный, но он раздаёт билеты с девяти утра и всего 200 в день. Во вторник Пиль пришёл туда в 6:20 утра.

Фирму основала Дженнифер Гофф. «Это был скорее эксперимент: наймут ли меня вообще», — говорит Гофф. Самый долгий заказ Пиля — 138 часов в очереди на громкое дело в Верховном суде.

Дядя Миша считает, что за 138 часов в очереди положена медаль.

Пиздато: субботнее утро больше не уходит на очередь.
Хуёво: чтобы ты выспался, кто-то встаёт в очередь в 6:20.

Мудрость дня: «Очередь никуда не девается — просто стоит на чужих ногах».

Professional line-standing becomes growing business as Americans seek to skip waits
January 16, 2026
(InvestigateTV) — If you don’t want to stand in line, you might be able to hire someone to do it for you.
A recent study found 85% of U.S. consumers wait in line at least a few times a month, and 65% describe negative emotions such as boredom, impatience and frustration from the experience.
Companies are now capitalizing on that frustration by offering professional line-standing services.
Rick Piel is a professional linestander in Washington, D.C.
When we tagged along with him on a recent gig, he arrived at the Washington Monument at 6:20 a.m. on a Tuesday morning.
He aims to be among the first people at the popular destination to secure free tickets that are released daily at 9 a.m. on a first-come, first-served basis.
“The line will get very long. There’ll be hundreds of people here and they only give out 200 tickets,” Piel said.
Piel works for Skip the Line, a Washington, D.C.-based company founded by Jennifer Goff in 2017. Goff started the business after noticing a massive line outside a “Game of Thrones” pop-up bar.
“It was more of an experiment to see if people would actually hire me,” Goff said. “But as soon as it happened, I just felt like this jolt of energy where I could really take this to the next level if I really worked really hard to do so.”
The company now employs a team of linestanders who wait for restaurant reservations, book signings, limited release product launches and general admission tickets to concerts and museums.
In Washington, D.C., frequent requests involve waiting for congressional hearings and Supreme Court cases with limited public seating.
Customers pay between $30 and $40 per hour for the service, with higher rates for overnight waits and during harsh weather conditions.
The home services platform TaskRabbit also offers waiting in line as a paid task. From 2023 to 2024, the company reported an 18% increase in bookings for that service nationwide.
Dr. Maggie Mulqueen, a Massachusetts-based psychologist, wrote an opinion piece for CNN in 2023 arguing there’s value in delayed gratification and questioning when waiting got such a negative reputation.
“I’m not saying everything is worth waiting for, but there are certain things in life that I think actually increase in value,” Mulqueen said. “I mean, if Christmas was every day, it wouldn’t be Christmas.”
Mulqueen expressed concerns about fairness and perceived inequities in society.
“We have commodified waiting so much that the people who don’t have to wait look down on the people who are waiting,” she said. “The haves and the have nots.”
Goff said her company emphasizes transparency about its services. For concerts, linestanders can hold spots for up to three people, and they inform those behind them in line.
“We always make sure clients know, hey, once you swap with us, please don’t bring 10 other people up front in line with you because it also hurts our business and our branding,” Goff said.
At the Washington Monument, other people waiting in line expressed no complaints about Piel’s paid service.
“It’s fine with me,” said Jerry Bennington, who was waiting in line. “I mean, you gotta make money somehow.”
Piel said his longest linestanding assignment lasted 138 hours for a high-profile Supreme Court case.
Skip the Line has also received requests for Fourth of July parade seating and even holding parking spots for clients.
